article_title: Integrating Topic Modeling and LLM Prompt Engineering into a Human-driven Approach to Analyze Interview Transcripts
citation: Teresa M. Ober, Karyssa A. Courey, Michael Flor. (2026). Integrating Topic Modeling and LLM Prompt Engineering into a Human-driven Approach to Analyze Interview Transcripts. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1.
title: Maintain human oversight throughout AI-assisted qualitative analysis to ensure contextual alignment and mitigate hallucination risk
description: The article's implications section holds that computational tools should augment rather than replace human interpretive work in qualitative analysis. As the authors state, "Human oversight remained essential throughout, ensuring contex- tual alignment and mitigating risks of hallucination or conceptual drift." The human-in-the-loop design positions researchers as validators of LLM outputs, reviewing labels for accuracy, relevance, and alignment with underlying sentence examples and bestwords.
requirements: Researcher judgment to validate and refine LLM outputs at each stage
Clear construct definitions embedded in prompts
constraints: The human-in-the-loop design mitigates but does not eliminate risks of hallucination and misalignment, and the interpretive process introduces subjectivity
target_learners: qualitative research teams adopting AI tools
target_learning_goals: rigorous and interpretable AI-assisted qualitative coding
examples: The research team reviewed all LLM-generated labels for accuracy and alignment, and no clear instances of hallucination were observed
key_sources: Teresa M. Ober, Karyssa A. Courey, Michael Flor. (2026). Integrating Topic Modeling and LLM Prompt Engineering into a Human-driven Approach to Analyze Interview Transcripts. Journal of Educational Data Mining, Volume 18, No 1. https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/1008

description: The glossary's human-centered perspective entry frames AI as working with humans and "helping to augment human skills". article_title: Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence
citation: UNESCO. (2022). Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence. UNESCO. https://www.unesco.org
title: Human rights and dignity as the cornerstone of AI ethics, with transparency, fairness and human oversight as fundamental principles
description: The Recommendation organizes AI ethics around a value-and-principle framework in which "the protection of human rights and dignity is the cornerstone", built on "fundamental principles such as transparency and fairness" together with "the importance of human oversight of AI systems". This framework serves as the normative foundation that the Recommendation's policy action areas then translate into practice across sectors including education and research.
requirements: Human oversight of AI systems as an operating condition of the framework

examples: The page presents the cornerstone-plus-principles structure as the basis of the 2021 Recommendation applicable to all 194 member states

article_title: AI Literacy in the Workforce
citation: Zachariah, I., Dallas, D., Ruiz, P., Liberman, B., & Karim. (2025). AI literacy for the Workforce. In Ruiz, P. et al. (Eds.), Implementing AI literacy across learning environments: A series of briefs. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/271
title: Design AI workplace integration with human intervention, review, and oversight to ensure ethical, responsible implementation
description: The brief holds that "AI workplace integration should include opportunities for human intervention, review, and oversight to ensure ethical and responsible implementation that complements human labor." This principle positions AI as complementing rather than replacing human expertise, supporting quality decision-making through suggestions, error identification, and data processing. It extends to hiring, where companies must evaluate and verify AI tools for fairness and bias mitigation while maintaining human oversight and transparency.
requirements: opportunities for human intervention, review, and oversight in AI workplace integration
constraints: future workers need to learn the ethics of responsible AI use and understand the risks of bias and discrimination that can result from AI implementation
target_learners: current and future workers crafting solutions and guardrails for AI use
target_learning_goals: ethics of responsible AI use
understanding risks of bias and discrimination in AI implementation
examples: The brief recommends companies implementing AI in hiring evaluate and verify these tools for fairness and bias mitigation, clearly explaining AI decision-making processes and their underlying logic

article_title: Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring
citation: Robinson, Carly D., David Gormley, Ana Trindade Ribeiro, and Susanna Loeb. (2026). Access is Not Enough: Human Support Improves Engagement with AI Tutoring. EdWorkingPaper No. 26-1451, Annenberg Institute at Brown University. https://edworkingpapers.com/ai26-1451
title: Provide human support alongside AI tutoring tools; access alone does not ensure meaningful student engagement
description: The article's central design recommendation is that schools deploying AI-based learning tools should not rely on access alone: providing access to an AI tutor, whether after school or during school hours, did not ensure meaningful engagement. Pairing the platform with an in-person tutor focused on engagement, motivation, and troubleshooting increased both usage and content completion, suggesting that "implementation and student engagement may be equally important determinants of impact" as technology quality. Human support may be especially important for students least likely to persist with AI-based learning on their own.
requirements: Tutors need standardized training designed to help them support students while using the AI platform, and sites need capacity to assign tutors to small groups.
constraints: The article states human-intensive models require additional personnel, training, and coordination; and human support increased engagement but usage remained well below the levels recommended for measurable reading gains.
target_learners: elementary school students, including economically disadvantaged students (>80% of the sample)
target_learning_goals: reading/literacy engagement with AI-delivered personalized instruction
examples: In both districts, treatment students met tutors in small groups of 2-5 for sessions including a 10-minute check-in, 15 minutes on the platform, and a 2-5 minute reflection; tutors did not provide direct reading instruction.

article_title: Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students
citation: García, E., Levin, H. (2025). Investing in Our Nation's Future: Advancing Educational Opportunity for Underserved Students. Los Angeles, CA: The Civil Rights Project/Proyecto Derechos Civiles, UCLA. https://escholarship.org/uc/item/29h9c9dn
title: Human capital theory as the framework linking education investment to productivity and societal returns
description: The report adopts human capital theory as its organizing framework, which "has established that education, or human capital more broadly, enhances a person's skills and increases productivity in the workplace, and that investments in education anticipate a wide range of benefits." The framework treats aggregate human capital as the nation's combined skills and attainment, weighted by demographic composition, and predicts both individual and collective economic gains, externalities, and nonmonetary benefits. The report cites empirical rates of return of about 10% for an additional year of education.
requirements: Requires treating education as an investment whose returns can be estimated and compared against costs
constraints: Returns estimates typically focus on increased earnings and the individual, though the report argues for broader accounting including externalities
target_learners: All students, with particular attention to those from historically disadvantaged racial/ethnic and income backgrounds
target_learning_goals: Educational attainment, skills, productivity, and long-term economic and social outcomes
examples: The report applies the framework to justify benefit-cost analysis of interventions from preschool through higher education.

article_title: Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human-AI co-regulation in learning
citation: S P, Joseph J, Jose M, S M A, N R and Joseph J (2026) Artificial intelligence as a cognitive partner: a developmental framework for human–AI co-regulation in learning. Front. Dev. Psychol. 4:1835258. https://doi.org/10.3389/fdpys.2026.1835258
title: Human–AI co-regulation framework: cognitive regulation is distributed between the learner and an external intelligent system
description: The article proposes that interactions with AI be conceptualized as a co-regulation process in which planning, monitoring, and control of cognition are shared between a human learner and an adaptive intelligent system. It integrates sociocultural theory, executive function and metacognition research, and distributed cognition, extending classical developmental accounts to non-human regulating partners. The authors state they "hypothesize that the interaction with AI can be viewed as a co-regulation process, where cognitive regulation is distributed between the learner and the external intelligent system."
requirements: An adaptive AI system capable of real-time response generation, feedback, and decision support, not merely passive information presentation
constraints: The framework is conceptual and not yet empirically validated; the authors note there are "still only limited empirical findings, which are frequently inconsistent"
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning
metacognitive development
problem solving
examples: The authors frame everyday AI use — organizing work, checking answers, generating descriptions — as analogous to guided participation traditionally associated with teachers or peers

article_title: AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning
citation: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337
title: Human–AI Coaching Game: coaching as a non-cooperative two-player POSG targeting independent competence
description: The Human–AI Coaching Game is a formal model casting AI coaching as a two-player partially observable stochastic game with distinct objectives for the two agents. The article argues that "coaching is fundamentally anon-cooperativegame" because "the learner seeks to maximize the task performance, while the coach optimizes a pedagogical objective, namely the learner'sindependentcompetence." The coach's reward is the Value of Independence (VoI): the learner's expected return acting without AI assistance. The learner's latent skill is private information the coach infers via a belief state. This contrasts with cooperative Assistance Games, which the article notes have been used almost exclusively for humans teaching robots.
requirements: A latent, totally ordered skill level for the learner that governs a skill-conditioned policy class
A coach reward measuring the learner's capacity for independent performance rather than assisted task performance
constraints: General POSGs are intractable, so the framework requires the reduction techniques of the L2C pipeline to be solvable
The VoI reward is counterfactual and expensive to estimate directly
target_learners: human learners of motor skills, primarily novices in the evaluated domain
target_learning_goals: long-term independent motor-skill competence rather than short-term assisted task performance
examples: The formalism is instantiated for FPV drone racing, where the coach maintains a per-gate belief over learner skill and blends expert and learner commands
key_sources: Wei Wang, Enlin Gu, Antonio Loquercio, Haimin Hu, Rahul Mangharam. (2026). AI Coaching for Accelerating Human Skill Development with Reinforcement Learning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.25337

article_title: Artificial Intelligence Driven Physics Assignments using Context Prompts
citation: Miguel Rodriguez and Peter Wulff. (2026). Artificial Intelligence Driven Physics Assignments using Context Prompts. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22578
title: Keep human oversight of AI assignments and design for transparency, flexibility, and manageable grading
description: The article recommends that instructors review or analyze saved AI conversations for common learning difficulties while retaining human oversight, since Gen AI can still produce inaccurate or misleading claims. It also advises focusing evaluation on student engagement and responses because AI-supported assignments generate a large amount of material to grade, and offering transparency and flexibility for students who hesitate to use AI for ethical reasons.

constraints: Paid AI versions may provide longer or more detailed responses than free versions, which can create inequality across students

examples: The authors note saved conversations can be reviewed directly or analyzed for common learning difficulties

article_title: Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence
citation: Jan Cvengros and Gerd Kortemeyer. (2026). Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-01606-4
title: Use human-in-the-loop AI grading with confidence-based selective filtering that defers uncertain cases to human graders
description: The article advocates a selective-prediction/deferral workflow in which the AI grades all student-items first and a confidence filter establishes "trust or distrust in these AI-judgements", accepting only reliable decisions and deferring higher-risk cases to humans. Filters include a partial-credit threshold, an IRT-based risk threshold, and exclusion by problem type. The authors argue this is essential because AI scores can exhibit undue confidence in ambiguous cases, and regulatory frameworks such as the EU's high-risk designation for AI in educational assessment mandate human oversight.
requirements: Confidence filter parameters must be adjustable based solely on risk tolerance, with stricter parameters rejecting more item-gradings and increasing human workload
A ground-truth-equivalent human grading workflow must remain available for deferred cases
constraints: The article states previous experiences show multimodal AI often succeeds in reading handwriting but still fails to interpret scientific diagrams and graphs, motivating exclusion of Drawing and Graphing parts
Filtering operates on AI scores alone, since in a production setting the ground truth would be unknown
target_learners: large-enrollment university students in general chemistry courses for non-majors
target_learning_goals: reliable scoring of open-ended handwritten exam responses including reaction equations, derivations, and explanations
examples: The study deployed the workflow in parallel with routine TA grading of a 15-page, 60-point, 46-part handwritten final exam, with students receiving only TA-assigned points
key_sources: Jan Cvengros and Gerd Kortemeyer. (2026). Assisting the grading of a handwritten general chemistry exam with artificial intelligence. Discover Artificial Intelligence. https://doi.org/10.1007/s44163-026-01606-4

article_title: ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education
citation: Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang. (2026). ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08040
title: Human-AI Collaborative IQ: education should cultivate learners' capacity to collaborate with AI rather than receive answers
description: Human-AI Collaborative IQ is the concept that "a new form of intelligence emerges when humans and AI systems collaborate effectively, and that education should cultivate this collaborative capacity." Under this view, AI should enhance the learner's own thinking and metacognition rather than deliver answers. ECNUClaw encodes the principle in its HEADS prompt templates, which prohibit direct answer-giving and prescribe Socratic questioning, grounded in Vygotsky's zone of proximal development with scaffolding gradually withdrawn as competence grows.
requirements: The companion must guide learners toward self-discovery through questioning rather than providing answers directly
target_learning_goals: Metacognitive development, self-discovery, and skills for collaborating with AI
examples: The HEADS base template includes the constraints "Never give direct answers. Use Socratic questioning to guide self-discovery" and "Help the learner develop skills for collaborating with AI, not dependency on AI"
key_sources: Yizhou Zhou, Jiayin Li, and Zhi Zhang. (2026). ECNUClaw: A Learner-Profiled Intelligent Study Companion Framework for K-12 Personalized Education. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.08040

article_title: A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers based on goals, models
citation: Finkelstein, N. (2026). A principled way to think about AI in education: guidance for educators and policy makers on action based on goals, models of human learning, and use of technologies. Draft manuscript, University of Colorado, Boulder.
title: Determine which educator and student activities remain human-led and which can be safely outsourced to AI technologies
description: The framework's central allocation principles state: "In our educational enterprise consider what domains of work are necessary or essential for educators to maintain as human led and directed, and what is feasible and safe to outsource to these new technologies", and in parallel determine which practices students must engage in as human-led and how technologies might advance learners' capacities. The article stresses these are not binary prescriptions: there are degrees of responsibility, and new responsibilities emerge as technologies develop.
requirements: Educators must enumerate the classes of action they control — objectives, content and skills development, habits of mind, motivation and community, curation, activity design, assessment and certification, continuous improvement — and judge each for human-led versus outsourced treatment
constraints: The article rejects absolutist framings such as replacing educators or students wholesale, calling them hyperbolic and reductionist
target_learners: higher education students and their instructors
target_learning_goals: preserving human-led development of higher-order capacities while productively leveraging AI tools
examples: The article suggests basic skills-based activities may be served by a computer tutor, while personalizing all interactions may undermine goals of socializing students and helping them regulate their own learning

article_title: Human-AI Co-Mentorship in Project-Based Learning: A Case Study in Financial Forecasting
citation: Freyaa Chawla, Ahan Chawla, Rishi Singh, Joe Germino, Grigorii Khvatskii. (2026). Human-AI Co-Mentorship in Project-Based Learning: A Case Study in Financial Forecasting. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.05144
title: Human-AI co-mentorship model with complementary tactical and strategic roles
description: The article proposes a co-mentorship model in which AI tools and human mentors play fundamentally different, complementary roles in project-based learning. AI provides "just-in-time tactical support: generating code scaffolding, suggesting hyperparameter ranges, and offering quick explanations of unfamiliar concepts," while human mentors frame problems, validate architectural decisions, and supply domain intuition and a complete project vision. The article states "The most effective co-mentoring configuration was rathercomplementary: AI handled routine implementation tasks, freeing human mentors to focus on higher-level reasoning, debugging and conceptual explanation."
requirements: Human mentors with domain expertise must remain available for strategic decisions, validation of AI outputs, and conceptual explanation.
constraints: Findings come from a single cohort of high-school and early-undergraduate students at US-style institutions over one summer; the authors caution against extrapolating to other contexts.
Findings are specific to the versions of LLM tools available during the summer of 2025.
target_learning_goals: research and programming skills
conceptual understanding of machine learning and finance
critical evaluation of AI outputs
examples: Daily stand-ups of around 30 minutes focused on problems to be solved, with students pursuing learning exercises between sessions, including dialogues with AI tools.

article_title: Comparative Validation of GPT-4o-mini and Teacher Mean Scores for Automated Scoring of Music Analysis Responses: Single-Pass Deployment, Repeatability, and Strategy-Specific Bias
citation: Baicheng Lin, Lingxi Jin, and Kyung-Seok Min. (2026). Comparative Validation of GPT-4o-mini and Teacher Mean Scores for Automated Scoring of Music Analysis Responses: Single-Pass Deployment, Repeatability, and Strategy-Specific Bias. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01783
title: Use LLM scoring of open-ended music analyses as a supplementary human-in-the-loop tool with strategy-specific calibration and dimension-level validation
description: The article recommends deploying LLM scoring as a supplement, not a replacement, for teacher judgment in music-analysis assessment. It proposes that "The LLM could provide preliminary scores or criterion-referenced feedback and flag responses that require further review," with teachers examining unusual score patterns, uncertain terminology, and large dimension discrepancies. Because prompting strategies produce distinct bias profiles and dimension-specific weaknesses, operational use requires calibration per strategy and validation per rubric dimension.
requirements: Strategy-specific calibration before operational use
Dimension-level validation rather than total-score agreement alone
Continued human oversight of flagged responses
constraints: Findings are from one model (GPT-4o-mini), one music-analysis task, one institutional context, and three runs at temperature 0.9; the article states they may not generalize to other models, tasks, sampling settings, institutions, or high-stakes assessment contexts
target_learning_goals: written music analysis covering harmonic analysis, formal structure, reasoning coherence, and music-theoretical terminology
examples: The study scored 300 undergraduate responses to a Mozart piano sonata analysis task with three teachers' mean scores as the reference, comparing Fs+CoT, RAG, and SC prompting strategies across Run1 and three-run aggregation conditions.

article_title: Revisiting the Performance of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Introductory Object-Oriented Programming
citation: Marina Lepp, Joosep Kaimre. (2026). Revisiting the Performance of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Introductory Object-Oriented Programming Assessments: Insights from 2026. https://orcid.org/0000-0003-3303-5245
title: Require careful human verification of GenAI-generated solutions for conceptually demanding object-oriented programming tasks
description: The article recommends that while contemporary GenAI systems can effectively support routine code generation, solutions involving more complex object-oriented reasoning need human checking. It states that GenAI systems "can effectively support routine code generation but still require caref ul human verification for conceptually demanding object -oriented programming tasks", because high overall scores do not translate into consistent performance on interfaces, abstract classes, and visual reasoning.
requirements: Instructors or reviewers must check GenAI solutions on conceptually demanding OOP topics such as interfaces, abstract classes, and visual program interpretation before relying on them.
constraints: The recommendation rests on evaluation of one Java-based introductory course's assessments, delivered in Estonian, with single first responses and no prompt engineering; the article notes AI assistants are highly sensitive to task phrasing and format.
target_learners: first-year university students in an introductory Java object-oriented programming course
target_learning_goals: object-oriented programming concepts including classes, inheritance, interfaces, and abstract classes
examples: Across the study's assessments, most models scored above the historical student cohort average, yet interfaces, abstract classes, and graphics-related questions continued to produce recurring errors.

article_title: A Framework for Institutional Change in the Age of AI
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A framework for institutional change in the age of AI. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00649-4
title: Privilege humble, local inquiries rather than scaling unevidenced AI practices
description: Because the evidence base for AI-based pedagogy does not yet exist, change efforts should surface and document localized uses of AI that show promise, share emerging cases without overclaiming generalizability, and aggregate these efforts to build future evidence. The article states: "Rather than advocating or scaling practices whose effectiveness has not been established, we should seek out and learn from localized uses of AI that show promise". Institutions should provide experimentation resources and access with guardrails without long-lasting commitments.
requirements: Resources for experimentation cycles, access to AI with guardrails, and mechanisms for sharing outcomes across the community
constraints: Scaling unevidenced practices risks exacerbating existing equity gaps, as learners with greater resources and digital literacy benefit first
target_learners: STEM faculty and institutional leaders in higher education
target_learning_goals: Developing responsible, pedagogically sound AI use while protecting student learning
examples: The SEI's grounded, course-level inquiry is re-purposed: AI inquiries are exploratory, aimed at generating insights rather than selecting evidence-based practices

article_title: The Intersection of Artificial Intelligence and Instructional Design Practice: A Systematic Review
citation: Pınar Nuhoğlu Kibar & Hale Ilgaz. (2026). The intersection of artificial intelligence and instructional design practice: a systematic review. Educational Technology Research and Development. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10624-z
title: Human–AI collaboration in instructional design: AI as co-worker, collaborator, and partner rather than a mere tool
description: The review synthesizes an emerging conceptualization in which AI is "not only regarded as a tool but was also conceptualised as a co-worker, collaborator, and partner within the instructional design process". It reports that human–AI collaboration leverages complementary strengths, with AI supporting personalization, content generation, feedback, and data-informed decisions, while "pedagogical intent, ethical judgment, and critical reflection remain human-centered responsibilities". The review positions AI predominantly as a collaborative assistant rather than an autonomous agent that augments human judgment and pedagogical reasoning.
requirements: Human expertise must remain central: contextual understanding, factual verification, and pedagogical soundness of AI outputs depend on designers' professional judgment
constraints: The review reports evidence regarding AI's added value in ID as emergent and context dependent, with few long-term, process-focused studies
target_learning_goals: effective integration of AI into instructional design processes

title: HUMAn: a simplified physiological model combining a heart-lung-brain interaction model with anatomical functional blocks to simulate real-time trauma patient evolution
description: HUMAn (Human is an Uncomplicated Model of Anatomy) is a simplified mathematical model of physiology that computes the real-time evolution of vital signs for trauma patients. Iterations led to a "heart-lung-brain interaction model coupled to functional blocks representing the main anatomical body parts"; these three organs were chosen because they are responsible for almost all the vital signs of the ABC evaluation performed by prehospital providers. Functional blocks divide the body into anatomical subsections, allowing traumas at different locations and localized treatments.

The model was required to be simple enough to allow real-time computation of all relevant vital parameters for several simulated patients simultaneously on regular computers or tablets
constraints: The current version was only developed to simulate traumas; other causes of major incidents, such as hazardous materials, cannot be simulated without further developments
Lack of pediatric-specific formulae prevents the generation of patients aged 16 years or younger
Absence of treatment-specific effects, which would be necessary to assess the effect of human and material resources through computer-based simulations
target_learners: prehospital providers, including paramedics and emergency physicians
target_learning_goals: major incident management training
simulating the time-based evolution of casualties during simulations
examples: Nine simulated patients were automatically generated with pathologies including massive internal hemorrhage, traumatic cardiac tamponade, complete left pneumothorax, burns, and head trauma to test the different systems and their interactions

title: Human-centered VR design framework of communication, form of reality, and presence applied to surgical simulator design
description: The article applies a human-centered VR design framework whose "High-level principles for human-centered VR design fall into three categories: communication, the form of reality, and presence." Communication requires prioritizing the UX with simple, transparent user-technology interaction to foster presence; form of reality concerns placement on the reality-virtuality spectrum and input/output hardware choices; presence manifests from the user's interpretation of immersion and is maximized by minimizing breaks in presence and optimizing world stability and depth cues. The authors used this framework to guide iterative refinement of the SurgiSim microscope UX/UI.
requirements: An iterative design process with regular end-user (surgeon) feedback to learn differences between VR and physical environments
constraints: Fundamental differences between physical and virtual worlds, such as gravity and the physical constraints of the Oculus headset and controllers, create challenges to the user's sense of presence
target_learners: surgeons and surgical trainees using VR simulation
target_learning_goals: surgical rehearsal skills
operating microscope maneuvering
microsurgery skills
examples: The thumbstick click to enter microscope view overcame the conflict between continuous head tracking and the need for a stable microscopic image; a proximity zone near the eyepieces for microscope mode was tested but expert feedback favored thumbstick activation
